newsitem.title: USA: FCC adopts auction rules for new wireless technology.
newsitem.headline: FCC adopts auction rules for new wireless technology.

text.p: Regulators adopted rules Tuesday for auctioning a valuable part of the airwaves that will be home to a wireless communications service that could give local phone and cable-TV companies a run for their money.

The Federal Communications Commission barred local phone companies and cable-TV firms from bidding for local multipoint distribution services (LMDS) licenses on their home turf for three years. The FCC wants to prevent them from snuffing out new rivals.
The FCC will auction 984 licenses nationwide. The total amount of specturm auctioned will be 1,300 megahertz.

LMDS is intended to allow consumers and businesses to zap voice, pictures and masses of data over high-speed wireless networks. Customers also could hook up to the Internet while bypassing traffic on the wired local phone network.
"We're going to cut out the local exchange carrier," said David Maloff, president of WebCel Communications Inc., a Washington, D.C.-based firm planning to bid at the FCC sale.
The technology is based on microwave signals that transmit data, voice and video within a three-mile radius. The signals are received by customers through a rooftop antenna.
The FCC hopes the rules "will open the door for a new broadband wireless service that will provide meaningful competition" to cable operators and local carriers.

The FCC also said it hoped the plan would provide enough additional radio spectrum to ensure the development of new wireless communication services for consumers and businesses nationwide. The auction is expected to occur this summer.
The agency also chose a flexible approach to the auction by not restricting the use of the airwaves to any particular service or application.
The FCC said that auction winners could be subject to certain public-interest obligations in the future.
